solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Like Farage's billionaire friend's vault – round

definitions.note: The possessive stops before its noun — the friend's money — so the definition points at what that fortune is made of rather than naming it.

blocks.note: a crypt is the vaulted chamber under a church
the letter drawn as a circle

explanation.surface: A billionaire pal of Nigel Farage has a strongroom, and it turns out to be a round one.
explanation.walkthrough: Reform UK is bankrolled by crypto billionaires, and the friend the clue means is one of them. 'Vault' is the burial chamber under a church here, not the gymnast's leap or the bank's strongroom.
explanation.definitionFit: The friend's fortune is held in cryptocurrency, and crypto is its everyday short name; the possessive leaves the noun — his money — unsaid.

clue.text: Revolting type of spin going over Braverman's head

indicators.note: To go over a thing is to pass right across it and cover it, so the word in front closes over the letter that follows.
A head sits at the front, so what is taken is the front letter of the name before it.

blocks.note: someone spinning on the spot is said to reel
the opening letter of the surname

explanation.surface: A piece of political spin so disgusting that it sails clean over Braverman's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' is wanted for one who revolts, not one who disgusts, which is the sense the surface pushes. A spin here is the giddy turn a person makes, which is what a body does when it reels.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebel is by definition someone in revolt, so the definition names the person by the act — against a crown, a party or a parent alike.

clue.text: "Putin's top occupier!" – Trump?

indicators.note: In a down clue the top of a word is where it starts, so only that opening letter is taken.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the name
whoever occupies a house is its resident

explanation.surface: A shout that Putin's chief land-grabber is Trump.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks and the dash stage a heckle and an answering question, and neither piece of punctuation carries an instruction. An occupier can hold a country or merely hold a flat.
explanation.definitionFit: Trump holds the office, so the clue names the answer by one man who has it — an example rather than a synonym, which is what the question mark concedes.

clue.text: Love poetry by wife: "Do some needlework"

blocks.note: love is nothing in tennis, and nothing is the round letter
verse is what poetry is written in
w is the wife on a genealogist's chart

explanation.surface: A wife hands over a love poem along with an order to get on with the sewing.
explanation.walkthrough: To oversew is to join two edges with stitches carried right over them, a real stitch rather than a coined word. The colon dresses the last three words as a quotation and has no job in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Oversewing joins two raw edges of cloth with stitches taken over the top of them, so anyone doing it is doing some needlework.

clue.text: Corporation, one beset by strike

indicators.note: To be beset by something is to have it closing in on every side, so the letter in front sits inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: a punch is a strike with the fist
a is the article that stands for a single one of a thing

explanation.surface: A company is under siege from a walkout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporation' for a belly is old British slang of the pompous sort — a man of substance with a corporation on him. 'One' is the article here rather than the Roman numeral, which is what buys the vowel.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporation is dated British slang for a fat stomach, the alderman's swelling front, and a paunch is exactly that.

clue.text: Pressure put on naff chat shows piece

indicators.note: Naff is British for shoddy and second-rate, and letters in a shoddy state are not standing in the order they should be.

blocks.note: p is pressure in a physics formula
four letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling rather than their sense

explanation.surface: Pressure is being piled on the makers of tacky daytime television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chat shows' looks like one noun and the clue cuts it in half, leaving the second word doing nothing but joining. A patch of ground, of cloth or of fog is a piece of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A patch is a piece — of cloth sewn over a hole, of land, of time — so the bare noun covers it with nothing stretched.

clue.text: Freakish large body on old bastard

blocks.note: the UN is the United Nations, about as large as a body of members gets
a natural was once the plain word for an illegitimate child, as in a natural son, and 'old' dates the usage

explanation.surface: A monstrous great body sitting on top of some ageing swine.
explanation.walkthrough: The UN turns up whenever a clue wants a large body, alongside the TUC and the EU. 'Bastard' reads as the insult and is wanted for the old legal sense, which is why the clue marks it as dated.
explanation.definitionFit: What is unnatural runs against nature, and a freak is precisely the thing nature was not supposed to produce.

clue.text: Conservative with a right load of rubbish as inducement

blocks.note: C is the Conservative on a British ballot paper
the article taken as a single letter
R is right on a stage direction or a set of instructions
rot is talking nonsense — 'what utter rot'

explanation.surface: A Tory talking a right load of nonsense dangles a sweetener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A right load of rubbish' is one British phrase and the clue takes it apart into three separate pieces. Only the last of them is a word in its own right; the other two are single letters doing quiet work.
explanation.definitionFit: The carrot of carrot-and-stick is the reward held out in front of someone to make them move, which is what an inducement is.

clue.text: Well, crooked Trump gets emasculated rotten

indicators.note: Something crooked has been bent out of its proper shape, and letters bent out of shape come out in another order.
To emasculate is to take the manhood out of a thing, so the letter that stands for male is the one dropped.

blocks.note: cor is the British exclamation of surprise, the 'well!' of 'cor blimey'
five letters of a surname, wanted for their spelling
M is male on any form, and that is the letter taken out

explanation.surface: A bent Trump is cut down to size, and the verdict is delivered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well' opens the sentence like a weary sigh and is quietly the first chunk of the answer. M for male is what an emasculation removes, a joke that works only because official forms print the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotten borough, a rotten copper, a rotten deal — rotten is the everyday word for morally decayed, which is what corrupt means.

clue.text: (& 10ac.) Parisian's "Hear! Hear!" for Mae West's forte

blocks.note: the cry is printed twice
the French verb to hear, so it is a Parisian's word for that cry

explanation.surface: A Paris crowd roars its approval in the way Mae West did best.
explanation.walkthrough: Mae West's whole act ran on lines carrying an innocent and an indecent reading at once. The French verb is the one buried in 'entendu', heard and understood, and it has to be translated before it is doubled.
explanation.definitionFit: Mae West built a career on remarks that could be taken two ways at once, so the double entendre was her speciality.

clue.text: see 9ac.
Chips all over Dicky's pretty underwear

indicators.note: Something spread all over a thing covers it completely, so the letters in front close right round the ones that follow.

blocks.note: chips are fries on an American menu
dicky is British for poorly — a dicky heart is a dodgy one

explanation.surface: Chips have been spilt all over a man called Dicky and his nice underthings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' wears a capital and looks like a name, and it is the British adjective for unwell. Chips and fries are the same potatoes on opposite sides of the Atlantic, which is what lets one word stand for the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Frillies is the affectionate British word for frilly knickers and slips, so 'pretty underwear' says what the drawer holds.

clue.text: The latest party gratuitous leader – grub!

indicators.note: A leader goes at the front, so the front letter of the word before it is all that is taken.

blocks.note: the hot ticket is the latest thing, the one everybody wants
a do is a party — the office do, a birthday do
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: The newest political party has an uncalled-for leader, and dinner is announced.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'do' for a party is British to the core, and it is the middle of three short pieces rather than the verb it looks like. The exclamation mark is a serving suggestion and carries no instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Grub is the casual word for food, and a hot dog is one thing it covers — street food standing as an example rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Bum wash

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes is the backside; the one wanted is the verb for cadging off other people
the reading the setter means: to clean something down with a soft pad

explanation.surface: Somebody is washing a backside.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are verbs, though 'bum' invites you to take it as the noun and picture the wrong end of a nurse's round. Two words are the entire clue, which is as short as a cryptic gets.
explanation.definitionFit: To sponge is to cadge money or drinks off others, which is bumming a fiver; and to sponge a floor or a patient is to wash it.

clue.text: "I'm unclear about ... about digits and the like

indicators.note: Something given as 'about' is only approximate, and letters that are only approximately right are not in the order handed over.

blocks.note: nine letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling rather than their sense

explanation.surface: Someone trails off in the middle of admitting the figures have defeated them.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks and the trailing dots stage a speaker losing the thread mid-sentence. The same small word shuffles the letters and then opens the definition, which is why it appears twice in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Numerical means having to do with numbers, and digits are numbers written down — the definition's first word supplies the 'concerning'.

clue.text: Female organisation rejected agent's cleaner

indicators.note: To reject a thing is to throw it back, so the word that follows is written back to front.

blocks.note: the WI is the Women's Institute, the British women's society of jam and Jerusalem
a rep is a sales agent, here written backwards

explanation.surface: A women's group has turned down the cleaning fluid a salesman was pushing.
explanation.walkthrough: The Women's Institute is the answer whenever a clue says female organisation, and it takes two letters. The cleaner wanted is the blade on a windscreen rather than a person with a mop.
explanation.definitionFit: A wiper is the blade that sweeps a windscreen clear, so it cleans — the thing doing the job rather than the person employed to.

clue.text: Fruit long associated with multinational

blocks.note: to pine for somebody is to long for them
Apple is the American computer giant, a multinational by any measure

explanation.surface: A fruit with a long history of ties to some global corporation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' is the verb to yearn rather than the adjective of duration, which is how a sentence about corporate history hides two whole words. Dole and Del Monte are the multinationals this fruit actually travels with.
explanation.definitionFit: A pineapple is the tropical fruit with the armoured skin and the tuft of leaves, so the bare word names its category.

clue.text: Pad out regal bust after measurement

indicators.note: A bust thing is broken, and broken letters will not stay in the order they were handed over in.
What comes after something is written behind it, so the shuffled letters land at the back of the measurement.

blocks.note: an en is the printer's measure, the width of a letter n
five letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling

explanation.surface: A royal statue's bust is being padded out once the measurements are taken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' is the sculpture the surface has in mind and the instruction to break things in the wordplay. The printer's en, half the width of an em, is a measure grids use constantly and typesetters gave up long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: To pad out a speech is to make it longer than it was, which is what enlarging anything does.

clue.text: Marriage that's likely to ignite?

definitions.note: The second half describes the answer instead of naming it — it says what the thing is apt to do — and the question mark owns up to the stretch.

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: a wedding, and the pairing off of two people that goes with it
the reading the setter means: the little stick that catches when it is struck

explanation.surface: A marriage with every chance of going up in flames.
explanation.walkthrough: A marriage is called a match because the two people are matched, the same word a matchmaker earns a living by. Five letters and five words make this the shortest clue in the puzzle bar one.
explanation.definitionFit: A match is a marriage or a pairing — 'a good match' — and a match is also the stick that bursts into flame when struck.

clue.text: Something to contain the shock of musical shown on web

blocks.note: Hair was the 1967 rock musical, the one with the nude scene
a net is a web of knotted mesh

explanation.surface: A musical streamed on the internet delivers a shock somebody wants contained.
explanation.walkthrough: A shock of hair is a thick unruly mop, and that is the shock being contained rather than a fright or a jolt. 'Web' is the knotted mesh, not the world wide one the surface offers.
explanation.definitionFit: A hair-net is the fine mesh a cook or a dancer pulls over a shock of hair to hold it flat, so the definition names it by the job.

clue.text: Hose used only by novelty sex beginners

indicators.note: What is used is no longer in the condition it left the shop in, and letters in that condition will not keep the order given.
A beginner stands at the start of things, so the starting letter of each word in front is what is taken.

blocks.note: four letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling
the opening letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Stockings worn only by people just starting out in novelty sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used only by' reads as a single restriction and the clue splits it, leaving the middle word as the pile. Hose is the draper's word for stockings, the one that survives in 'hosiery'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hose is the trade's old collective for stockings, and nylons are the stockings themselves — a definition by material.

clue.text: Defector to take legal action against Labour leader and city

indicators.note: A leader stands at the head of things, so only the first letter of the word in front of it is taken.

blocks.note: to sue somebody is to take them to court
the opening letter of the party's name
LA is Los Angeles, shortened the way Americans say it

explanation.surface: A turncoat is taking the head of the Labour Party and an entire city to court.
explanation.walkthrough: Braverman, the Conservative home secretary who crossed to Reform UK in January 2026, is the defector the definition means. Her surname turns up in another clue in this puzzle, which is how a bare first name stays fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Suella Braverman quit the Conservatives for Reform UK in January 2026, so her first name alone answers to 'defector'.

clue.text: Arrogance of one involved in brush-off

indicators.note: Whatever is involved in something is caught up inside it, so the letter goes within the letters alongside.
Milk that has gone off is not what it was sold as, and letters that have gone off will not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: five letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: The self-importance of somebody on the receiving end of a snub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brush-off' is one hyphenated noun in the surface and two jobs in the wordplay, the first word being the pile and the second the instruction. The Greeks used the answer's word for the pride that invites punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: Hubris is overweening pride, the self-importance that walks a man into disaster, so arrogance is its plain English.

clue.text: Slippery Cyclops is grabbed by familiar film star

indicators.note: Whatever is grabbed by somebody ends up in their grip, so the letters in front go inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: Sly is what everyone calls Sylvester Stallone
the setter writing of himself says I'm

explanation.surface: The setter has been seized by a film star he is on first-name terms with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Familiar' is the instruction to use the nickname rather than the full name, which is how a Hollywood surname shrinks to three letters. Cyclops is this crossword's setter, so he can put himself in his own clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Slippery and slimy both describe the man you cannot get a straight answer out of, as well as the surface you cannot keep your feet on.

clue.text: Labour pursuing poor Ian –  "not cool"

indicators.note: A poor effort has not come out as it should, and letters that have not come out as they should are in the wrong order.
To pursue is to come along behind, so the word in front of it lands at the back of the answer.

blocks.note: three letters for the pile, wanted for their spelling
to labour at a job is to sweat over it

explanation.surface: The Labour Party is chasing some hard-up bloke called Ian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' wears a capital and looks like the party, and it is the plain verb for toil. The quotation marks round the definition flag slang: what is not cool here is a person panicking, not a temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody in a sweat is flustered and anxious, the opposite of cool in the sense of calm and collected rather than chilled.

clue.text: Grass poses question about Farage's end

indicators.note: To put one thing about another is to wrap it round, so the question word closes over the single letter that follows.
The end of a name is its final letter, so that one letter is all the name gives up.

blocks.note: what is the word a bald question is posed with
the last letter of the surname

explanation.surface: A police informer is asking questions about how Farage finishes up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' is the informer the surface wants and the plant the definition means. The answer is a cereal, and cereals are grasses botanically, which is what makes so bare a definition fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheat is a cereal, and cereals are members of the grass family — the botanist's sense of the word rather than the lawn or the informer.

clue.text: (& 27ac.) Choice person's first step that's soon abandoned by incoming government?

definitions.text: that's soon abandoned by incoming government?
definitions.note: The definition is a relative clause rather than a noun: it says what becomes of the answer instead of naming it, and the question mark admits the jibe.

indicators.note: The first of a word is the letter it opens with, so that single letter is all that is taken.

blocks.note: a choice is a choosing, and the formal noun for picking people by vote is wanted
the opening letter of the word
a ledge is the narrow shelf a climber steps onto

explanation.surface: The first move a new person makes is dropped the moment the government changes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Choice' is the act of choosing rather than the thing chosen, which is what lets one short word carry eight letters. The definition runs on into 27 across and is a jibe at Westminster rather than a dictionary sense.
explanation.definitionFit: An election pledge is a promise made while campaigning, and the clue defines it by its fate: the incoming government quietly drops it.

clue.text: see 26ac.
Very brave Ed on party's fringe?

indicators.note: A fringe is the edge of a thing, so the letter standing at the edge of the word in front is the one taken.

blocks.note: Ed Balls was Labour's shadow chancellor, better known since for television
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Ed is hovering at the edge of the party and showing some nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the surname: a politician's name doubles as the crude word for nerve. Party conferences hold fringe meetings round the edges, which is the fringe the surface is pointing at.
explanation.definitionFit: To be ballsy is to have guts, the vulgar British word for courage — stronger than plain brave, which is the work 'very' is doing.

clue.text: Agreement to go outside to get stuffed?

indicators.note: To be outside something is to stand round it on every side, so the word in front closes over the letters that follow.

blocks.note: a go at something is a try
eating your fill is what leaves you stuffed

explanation.surface: An agreement to step outside for an enormous dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get stuffed' is the British brush-off and also what a large meal does to you, and only the second sense is wanted. 'Go outside' reads as an invitation to fight, which is the picture the mechanism quietly ignores.
explanation.definitionFit: A treaty is a formal agreement between states, so the bare noun covers it with nothing stretched.
